chunks: A number of our companions, from Sahl bin Ziyad, and Ali bin Ibrahim, from his father, and Muhammad bin Yahya, from Ahmad bin Muhammad, from Ibn Mahboub, from Ali bin Raib, from Al-Halby, who said:

I asked Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) about a man who performed *li'an* (cursing) with his wife while she was pregnant, and her pregnancy had become evident. So he denied what was in her belly. So when she gave birth, he claimed her child and confessed to it, and claimed that it was from him. He (peace be upon him) said: 'His child is returned to him, and he inherits him, and he is not whipped, because the *li'an* has passed.'

key_terms.لَعَنَ: To perform li'an (cursing), a specific judicial procedure in Shia jurisprudence where a husband denies paternity of his wife's child.

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a husband who denies paternity during his pregnant wife's pregnancy but admits it after birth?
ai.summary: This narration from al-Kafi clarifies the procedural finality of *li'an* in Shia jurisprudence, establishing that once the husband admits paternity after the child's birth, the child is legally attributed to him and inherits from him. Crucially, the Imam rules that the husband is exempt from the *hadd* punishment of whipping because the *li'an* ceremony itself has already been consummated, rendering the subsequent admission a confirmation rather than a reversal of the curse. This highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on the procedural integrity of the *li'an* ritual over the finality of paternity determination.
